title: Introduction
introduction: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) serve as critical security components for identifying potentially malicious network activities (Denning, 1987). This study presents a comparative analysis of machine learning techniques for binary classification of network traffic using the NSL-KDD benchmark dataset, comparing ensemble methods, non-linear classifiers, and support vector approaches.

sections.title: Background and Problem Statement
sections.content_html:
Traditional signature-based intrusion detection systems fail against zero-day exploits and novel attack vectors that do not match existing signatures. Machine learning offers an alternative by enabling systems to learn patterns from data and generalize to detect previously unseen attack variants (Buczak & Guven, 2016).

The NSL-KDD dataset, introduced by Tavallaee et al. (2009), addresses limitations of the original KDD Cup 1999 dataset by removing duplicate records and providing balanced attack representation. It contains 125,973 training instances with 41 features (expanding to 121 after encoding), partitioned into DoS, Probe, R2L, and U2R attack categories.

Key Challenges:

  • Class Imbalance: The training set contains 53.46% attacks while the test set has 56.98%, requiring class-weighted learning strategies and appropriate evaluation metrics (Chicco & Jurman, 2020).
  • Novel Attack Detection: The test set intentionally includes attack types absent from training data, simulating real-world zero-day detection challenges.
  • Evaluation Metrics: Standard accuracy can be misleading for imbalanced datasets. This study employs Balanced Accuracy, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), Attack Detection Rate, and False Alarm Rate for comprehensive evaluation.

sections.title: Research Objectives
sections.content_html:
This study pursues the following objectives:

  1. Compare representative classifiers from three algorithm families—ensemble methods (BaggingClassifier), non-linear methods (DecisionTreeClassifier), and support vector methods (RidgeClassifier).
  2. Apply systematic hyperparameter optimization using 5-fold cross-validation.
  3. Assess performance using multiple metrics including Balanced Accuracy, MCC, and Attack Detection Rate.
  4. Conduct bias-variance decomposition to characterize error sources for each model.
  5. Provide practical recommendations for deploying ML-based intrusion detection.

Scope: Binary classification (normal vs. attack) using supervised learning on NSL-KDD. Multi-class categorization and deep learning approaches are outside scope.

sections.title: Literature Review
sections.content_html:
The foundations of intrusion detection trace to Anderson (1980) and Denning (1987), who established frameworks for detecting anomalous behavior. The KDD Cup 1999 dataset catalyzed research progress, with NSL-KDD subsequently addressing its duplicate record issues (Tavallaee et al., 2009).

Classical Machine Learning Approaches: Decision Trees (Quinlan, 1986; Breiman et al., 1984) achieve competitive accuracy while producing interpretable rule sets. Ahmad et al. (2018) demonstrated that tree-based methods consistently outperform linear classifiers on NSL-KDD. Ensemble Methods (Breiman, 1996, 2001) combine multiple classifiers to reduce variance and improve generalization—Aburomman & Reaz (2017) provide a comprehensive survey of ensemble approaches for IDS. Support Vector Methods (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995) find optimal separating hyperplanes, with Ridge regularization (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970) preventing overfitting; however, their effectiveness depends critically on feature space linear separability.

Recent Advances (2019-2024): Liu & Lang (2019) surveyed machine learning and deep learning methods for IDS, identifying random forests and gradient boosting as top-performing classical approaches. Sarker (2021) provided an algorithmic perspective emphasizing the importance of model selection based on problem characteristics. Thakkar & Lohiya (2023) conducted a comprehensive survey covering feature selection, performance metrics, and application challenges—notably advocating for MCC and balanced accuracy over simple accuracy for imbalanced datasets. Alrowais et al. (2023) explored hybrid optimization approaches, though concluded that traditional ensemble methods remain competitive baselines.

Evaluation Methodology: Matthews Correlation Coefficient has emerged as the preferred metric for imbalanced classification (Matthews, 1975; Chicco & Jurman, 2020). ROC-AUC analysis with DeLong's test (DeLong et al., 1988) provides statistical comparison of classifier discrimination. The bias-variance framework (Geman et al., 1992) guides understanding of model generalization, with bagging proven to reduce variance while preserving bias (Breiman, 1996). Cross-validation with stratification ensures reliable performance estimates (Kohavi, 1995).

Research Gap: While extensive literature compares individual algorithms, few studies provide systematic bias-variance decomposition alongside traditional metrics. This study addresses this gap by combining comprehensive multi-metric evaluation with bootstrap-based bias-variance analysis to characterize error sources for each model family.

sections.title: Overview of Machine Learning Models
sections.content_html:
Three team members independently investigated different algorithm families:

Muhammad Usama Fazal (TP086008) - BaggingClassifier (Ensemble): Implements Bootstrap Aggregating with 150 decision tree estimators (Breiman, 1996). Reduces variance by training on bootstrap samples and combining predictions through majority voting. Configuration: 85% max sample ratio, balanced class weights.

Md Sohel Rana (TP086217) - DecisionTreeClassifier (Non-Linear): Recursively partitions feature space using Gini impurity criterion (Breiman et al., 1984). Provides interpretable decision rules with O(log n) prediction complexity. Configuration: max_depth=20, balanced class weights.

Imran Shahadat Noble (TP087895) - RidgeClassifier (Linear): Applies L2-regularized least squares to classification (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970). Assumes linear separability—exhibits high bias when true boundaries are non-linear. Configuration: balanced class weights, default regularization.

sections.title: Document Structure
sections.content_html: Chapter 2 details methodology including data preprocessing and evaluation metrics. Chapter 3 presents results with bias-variance analysis. Chapter 4 describes individual contributions. Chapter 5 concludes with recommendations.
